correctness.rationale: Cai–Kiah–Nguyen–Yaakobi Proposition 9 Type-A theorem identifies exactly those distinct word pairs with two shared one-deletion descendants as alternating opposite-phase swaps on unique intervals. Each interval produces one neighbor, so degree is sum of maximal alternating-suffix excess R_j. Appending a letter gives exhaustive transitions t→1, t→2, t→t+1 and the claimed positive degree-polynomial recurrence for every integer q≥2. For independent uniform q-ary letters, P(R_j≥k)=(q-1)q^{-k}, E R_j=1-q^{-(j-1)} and E(R_{j+1}|past)=p+q^{-1}R_j. This yields exact covariance q^{-(j-i)}Var(R_i), the finite mean/variance, and asymptotic coefficient 2(q+1)/(q-1)^2. A common reset state of probability 1/q and geometric tails provide stationary ergodicity, bounded fourth moments, conditional variance law and martingale Lindeberg; centering and negligible weighted martingale correction yield the fixed-q CLT. Independently reconstructed deletion-ball graph and all interval counts for q=2, n≤7 and q=3,n≤5; all individual degrees and exact means matched. Analytic recursion and mixing proof, not finite tests, establish all lengths.

evidence: Cai Type-A universally characterizes local pairs; the q-ary distribution and Gaussian variance require counting overlaps under an IID word model.

value.rationale: The distribution of source-word ambiguity degrees is a natural invariant of the q-ary two-read reconstruction channel, different from the global edge count. All q-ary alphabets and all lengths plus exact finite spread and explicit Gaussian scale give usable local-degree statistics for degree-sensitive code/design analysis. The fact that q=2 is known does not make the substantive q≥3 extension intrinsically worthless.

limitations: The q=2 component and all-q mean are already covered, so novelty only for genuine q≥3 distribution/variance/CLT.
Classical alternating-pattern renewal statistics could yield q-ary mean/variance under another name.
For q growing with n and multi-deletion or repeated-read multiplicities the theorem makes no claim.
